speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, not at the moment, if the hon. member does not mind. I would be glad to receive his question when I have concluded my initial remarks. As I said, we are concerned about unanswered questions. We want to know about the question of tax shelter, of public disclosure, about interlocking directives, about the possibility of insider information, and so on.
A serious question is at issue. If the bill were to pass it would anticipate the legislative decision parliament should properly make in revising the Bank Act when a full examination of the future of banking and financial institutions can be made. The Bank Act is reviewed every so often, and I understand the next review will be next year. This bill provides for exemptions which negate the Bank Act. If the bill passes, you might as well say the Bank Act does not exist. I know that certain agreements have been reached with the powers that be. I do not suppose the company is doing anything illegal. I do not suggest for a moment that it is. Nor am I trying to say anything about IAC shares. But we wonder who exactly is interested in this IAC conversion. We have embarked on many long discussions in committee. I have talked privately with the IAC people and with the sponsor of the bill who has been a good advocate on their behalf, and I realize that we cannot take this matter lightly.
Here is a large, important Canadian company coming to parliament and asking for something to be done on its behalf. Let me say that we would like to help. We are not refusing to help; that is not our attitude. We should like to be persuaded of the worthiness of their cause so that we can accommodate them. We are open to any argument any hon. member may want to put forward. We know the importance of what we are doing. We are not doing it casually, and we are not delaying anything. My colleagues and I have discussed this among ourselves and we are persuaded that there must be a fight on this question. As I say, we will listen to arguments, and if someone makes an argument showing that this conversion is in the national interest we will look at it. Let me say this: it is the strategy of the government to let the opposition talk itself out. Well, we will not talk ourselves out. We will need to be persuaded out, if I may put it that way, so hon. members might as well get up and say what they must say either in defence of or against the bill.
The Bank Act must be revised. It is significant that not one of the chartered banks appeared before the committee to say, "We do not want another competitor" or, "We think there is something wrong with what is going on." There was a conspiracy of silence. Not all committee members have been so silent. This matter is something of a precedent. We must consider the Bank Act and the implications of the Bank Act. As I say, if this bill passes in its present
March 11, 1976

form there will, in effect, have been a revision of the Bank Act. That, exactly, is what will have happened. I suggest that one cannot lightly pass a bill whose effect will involve a revision of the Bank Act.
We should not pass a bill of this importance so lightly. It has not been given more than cursory attention by a committee of this House. A few witnesses were called. There were hearings and meetings in the Senate, and I believe there were four references in the debates of the other place to this question. There were few committee hearings into a bill of such complex and enormous implications. There were some hearings in the House of Commons committee. Nevertheless, not one of us would dream of amending the Bank Act in this manner. You cannot, by hearing a few witnesses and saying, "Yes, we know all about it; we understand the situation exactly", amend the Bank Act by passing this bill. Interestingly enough, there are two senators who in fact are directors of banks: Senator Molson and Senator Desruisseaux.

speechtext: Only two?

Those are the only two on the committee. There may be others; we did not look into that. The point is that both these senators declared in committee their conflict of interest and said they could not vote on the bill. Nevertheless, they did not consider it a conflict of interest to say it was a very good idea that the IAC conversion into the Continental Bank go ahead. What strikes me about this whole thing is the coziness. For instance, Senator Mac-naughton went out of his way, whenever questions were raised, to say, "We have to get this through as these boys are in a hurry." When we held it up, he indicated solicitude by asking how much time we needed. He emphasized that the thing was to get it pushed through. If it were a minor bill being dealt with in the face of some national emergency or some compelling interest, I would not be reluctant to see it expedited through this House. There is no reason to argue against that. However, it is a bill that raises all kinds of questions. There are more unanswered questions than questions that have been answered. It should not go through without serious consideration on the part of the House of Commons.
I see that Your Honour is about ready to remind me how the clock works. I appreciate that hint. I have other things I would like to say, but I am sure my colleagues will be only too happy to enlarge on them. There was a question being directed to me. I would appreciate it if Your Honour would permit that question.

Mr. Speaker, I was not on the committee, as was the hon. member. The only thing I did was read the brief. Therefore, I am asking this question to solicit information. As I take it, in the transition from IAC to the Continental Bank, the problem of transition, which is sometimes normal when there is an amalgamation of trust
Continental Bank of Canada
companies-and I have had some experience in this-is that they are trying to keep the same directors for the bank as with IAC, and that is why they have had to have this change in certain sections. If IAC were ready to compromise and waive that, would the hon. member then see things in a different light?

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
It would certainly improve the light, Mr. Speaker, but there are a lot of other questions. We have ten amendments, so this is not our only objection. The hon. member is quite correct. It is a question of what kind of assets you transfer. Two general kinds of assets are now held by IAC. Some are eligible assets for a bank to hold, and some are ineligible assets. The question of an amendment to the Bank Act arises in permitting the ineligible assets to be transferred to Continental Bank and dissipated or used up over a period of ten years. Although they will not all be used up over that period, it is anticipated they can use enough to at least make it manageable at the end of that ten-year period. This is what the chartered banks have been asking us for a long time-the right to hold and to deal in these kinds of ineligible assets. This is the kind of thing the Bank Act has refused to give them. This is more properly the province of other financial institutions.
Our concern is simply this: if we grant this sanction to the IAC-and, admittedly, IAC has no real, practical way of transforming these present assets into a bank without this special agreement-where does that leave us with regard to the Bank Act? The banks would say we did the right thing with IAC-in fact, they are saying it now-and surely we could do the right thing for them. We will have created-this will be confirmed at a later date-a precedent that will be looked upon by everyone in the industry. Certain competitors of IAC see it that way. The quietness of the banks, their unwillingness to say anything at all except indirectly, as they did in the other House and in a private capacity, is a clear indication there would be great joy in the boardrooms of the banking institutions if this bill passes.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), I will try to be brief because I would very much like to see the bill proceed through this reading to enactment. I want to reflect upon the observations of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) that this is not a bill which they are prepared to let be talked out. They intend to carry on the debate as long as they feel it is necessary for their purposes. What I want to do, in very brief compass, is appeal to the sense of fairness of the hon. members of the New Democratic Party.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge took a considerable amount of his time today to develop the allegations that there may have been some advance knowledge by certain shareholder groups about the bank application. I am not familiar with the details of the structure of the company. However, I listened to what he said and listened to the allegations which are very serious and which might at least give rights to the vendors of the interest that he referred to to have their sales set aside and reacquire the shares and perhaps rights under the provincial securities legislation. But, after laying all that out, he then indicated he is not questioning the propriety of it.

March 11, 1976
Continental Bank of Canada
I attended a couple of the committee meetings. As a result of the questions that were asked and the forthright replies that were given, I took it that this House ought to be satisfied there is no impropriety relating to acquisition of the shares in question. I very much regret hearing the hon. member referring to the issue again. I was surprised at the end of it to hear him say that is not an issue as far as he is concerned.
I want only to make three points. I think it is totally unfair to hold up the bill on the basis of these three points. First, he stated that there was a failure of the government or of this parliament to enact a general procedure for the incorporation of banks. We have had such a bill kicking around for a long time. It is regrettable that the bill has not yet been brought into law. If it had been, this whole procedure might well be unnecessary, although there are a lot of aspects of this incorporation which would be looked at in the course of reincorporation. They would have been looked at in some other way if that bill had been brought forward.
I want to argue that the NDP, if anyone, should know how scarce the time of this parliament is, how important it is that we try to organize our time better and that all sides of the House try to co-operate with that objective so that it would be possible to get more legislation considered in this chamber. Certainly, if we had other rules an allocation of time or a better spirit of co-operation among all parties it might well have been possible to have had that banking bill made law by now. In any event, I argue that it is totally unfair for these applicants to be made the whipping-boy for the failure of parliament to deal with that legislation and make it law.
Second, the hon. member raised some objections, which I share, with regard to members of the Senate serving as bank directors. In the case of the banking group which is before us, if what he says is true-and I do not question it-there are some senators who will be directors of the new bank. That may well be agreed to be improper, but there are other banks which have senators as directors.

speechtext:
I accept, of course, the hon. member's statement, but in view of what he says I think his criticism is even more unfair. We have before us innocent applicants who do not include Senators, and they are being made the whipping boy for a standard of conduct by Senators to which the NDP, or at least the hon. member, objects. I do not think it is fair that an application which is otherwise valid should be held up and debate prolonged because some other standard ought to be imposed in the other place governing the conduct of Senators. I would urge the hon. member to withdraw his objection to this application on that ground.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would argue that he is using this application as a whipping boy for the whole capitalist

system. He does not believe it is in the public interest as a whole for banks "to do their thing," if I can put it that way, and participate in the market place in a way they consider to be in their own interests. We believe that the public interest is served by private corporations operating toward private objectives. He may have a great many complaints about the banking system in Canada and about whether the banks work well for us, but he has not said anything to indicate that this bank will work in any worse way than the others.
If the hon. member has an objection to the banking system it should not be used to prevent a new bank from coming on the scene and participating as a bank in the market place. If our banks have not served Canada well, that certainly is not something that should be laid at the doorstep of IAC and the new Continental Bank which hopefully is to be shortly incorporated.
For my part, although I think the banking system has flaws, it is an industry that is constantly under review by government and is reviewed every ten years by parliament. On the whole I think Canadians have good reason to be proud of their banks and the role they play in the development of our country. If he has objections to them, again I urge the hon. member not to use those objections as a means of preventing this particular worth-while application from proceeding.

subsubtopic: CONTINENTAL BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a proposal to permit establishment of a new bank to join the banks we already have in our country. This application comes at a very interesting time. I am not surprised that some new group wants to get part of the action because bank profits have been rising very sharply, by anywhere from 25 to 50 per cent per year, over the past three or four years. Last week in fact the Toronto Globe and Mail reported that bank profits for the previous quarter had increased by 35 per cent over the same period a year earlier.
It is somewhat ironic, to put it mildly, that the newspaper reports which indicated that bank profits for that quarter were up by 35 per cent also indicated that this, what I consider to be massive increase in profits, was within the guidelines established by the Anti-Inflation Board.
The Government of Canada is proposing, and parliament is approving, legislation that restricts the increase in wages and salaries which most citizens in Canada will be able to receive, which interferes with the free collective bargaining system as we have known it. The legislation, in effect, says to any group of workers that they may not get an increase in wages in 1976 of more than 10 per cent over what they received in 1975 except under very special circumstances, which have never really been spelt out by the government in the law or regulations, or in any kind of detail by the Anti-Inflation Board.
In the city of Winnipeg the transit workers are on strike. These workers run the buses upon which so many people depend; workers need them to go to work and senior citizens depend on them to visit friends and relatives. These workers have been on strike for over 7 weeks because the city of Winnipeg has said that its interpretation of the Anti-Inflation Board ruling is that these transit
March 11, 1976

workers cannot receive more than a 9.5 per cent wage increase. Indeed the city of Winnipeg will not even agree to let a higher proposal go to the Anti-Inflation Board for a ruling. Yet the banks had an increase in profits during the last quarter of 35 per cent over the same period in 1974, and this is within the guidelines set by the Anti-Inflation Board. I am therefore not surprised that we have an application from a group that wants to establish a new bank. I am only surprised that we do not have more applications. Why should not a group of well to do citizens in Canada want to get in on what is obviously a very lucrative kind of enterprise?
The question we have to ask ourselves is not whether this is good business for this particular group of directors and shareholders of IAC. Unlike the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) who has just spoken, who obviously follows the precept of the famous-or rather infamous- Charlie Wilson of the United States, who on one occasion said that what is good for General Motors is good for the country, we believe that what is good for IAC is not necessarily good for the people of Canada. We want to know what the benefits will be to the people of Canada from this new bank before we approve its establishment.
Similarly I should like to believe that the owners of IAC will at least have to live by the same rules and laws as all other banks, in accordance with the Bank Act. I see no reason to hurry this, Mr. Speaker. I do not believe that the people of Canada will be at all harmed if this matter stands over. If the directors and shareholders of IAC cannot qualify as a bank under the present regulations set out in the Bank Act, then I think representations should be made on their behalf when the Bank Act undergoes its regular revision which takes place every ten years, and which I think is due in 1977.
As I say, I do not believe there will be much harm done to the ordinary people of this country if IAC has to wait until 1977 when perhaps its directors will be able to persuade-and they may be right-the majority of the members of this parliament that the Bank Act as we know it at present should be revised so that IAC, a financial corporation, is able under the regular standard provisions of the act to change its organization and become the Continental Bank, a bank that will need no special consideration or exemptions from the parliament of Canada.
I cannot accept the suggestion by the hon. member for York Centre that we ought to pass a bill which was designed substantially to meet the needs, not of the people of Canada, but of the shareholders and the directors of IAC.
The purpose of this bill is to establish a new bank which will be able to take all the assets and operations of IAC Limited, with some exceptions, and operate them as a bank. One of the problems which IAC is currently having is that, because it is not a bank, the leverage on its money, the multiple of its assets that it can loan out to customers, or more simply, the number of times it can turn over its money in the form of loans and mortgages, is much lower than that of the chartered banks.
Normally trust companies, according to the testimony before the Commons finance committee, achieve a leverage
Continental Bank of Canada
ratio of about 6 to 1. IAC, because it is the largest Canadian controlled finance company, with huge assets and a reputation for careful management, has been able to achieve a leverage ratio of some 7 to 1 on its money. This is considered high for such financial institutions, but it is much lower than the chartered banks achieve: they are in the range of 25-35 to 1. This is because of the prestige involved in the status of chartered banks, and also because the chartered banks are more closely watched and more closely regulated by the Bank Act than are some other financial institutions. So there is a lot of money involved, all other things being equal, in being a chartered bank.
Basically, then, IAC has grown as big as it is likely to get unless it is allowed to convert itself into a bank. In recent years, since the Bank Act revisions of 1967, the banks have been growing faster than other types of financial institutions. Figures prepared by Statistics Canada indicate that the banks have outstripped all other financial institutions in terms of asset growth and consumer loans.
Looking at the annual average growth rates for the years between 1964 and 1974 we see that the chartered banks showed an annual growth rate of 17.5 per cent; credit unions, 17.3 per cent; trust companies, 15.9 per cent; mortgage loan companies, 13.6 per cent; trustee pension funds, 12.4 per cent; fire and casualty companies, 11.2 per cent; sales finance and consumer loan companies, 10.9 per cent; and life insurance companies, 8.2 per cent.
In an area of particular significance to IAC-consumer credit-the growth of the banks has been even greater. This is illustrated by the figures for the years between 1964 and 1974 where the percentage increase has been as follows: chartered banks, 19.8 per cent; credit unions, 14.6 per cent; retail dealers, 7 per cent; sales finance and consumer loan companies, 4.5 per cent. In other words the banks had an average annual growth of almost twice as much as the average for all business institutions. It is no wonder the directors of IAC would like to convert that corporation into a bank.
One of the advantages the banks have is that they are deposit-taking institutions. They can bring in money at relatively small interest rates and loan it out at an interest rate that brings them in a steady profit but is lower than that of the other types of financial institutions such as IAC, which has to get its money through notes and debentures at a higher cost than that of the banks. IAC, in other words, has to borrow its money, sometimes from the chartered banks themselves, and loan it out at a higher rate, and the spread on the rates is its source of profit.
The banks, paying relatively low interest rates on deposits and no interest on a great deal of the money that comes in in the form of deposits, have a secure and steady source of low cost money that is not available to IAC. As I said earlier, it is no wonder that IAC would like to get into the act. As one of the officers of the bank replied in the Finance Committee a few weeks ago, "We want to play in the major leagues". There is no doubt that moving into the major leagues would be immensely profitable for IAC and its shareholders. That is enough reason for them to approve the bid to convert into a bank. But shareholders' profit is not a reason that should be so compelling to parliament. In order for parliament to pass this bill it should satisfy itself

March 11, 1976
Continental Bank of Canada
that the bill is in the public interest. That, it would appear, is difficult to do.
IAC Limited was first known as Industrial Acceptance Corporation when it was set up in Windsor in 1925. Its business at that time was almost wholly dealer loans, lending money to car dealers to finance their inventory of new cars. Its business, in other words, was in commercial loans rather than consumer loans. It stayed primarily in this business for several years, and is still in it, but over the years it has broadened its base to other financial activities. It is now involved in wholesale and retail sales financing, dealer loans and business loans, mortgages for both homes and businesses, leasing of capital equipment, and consumer loans. In fact most of its advertisements in recent times have dealt with other aspects of business rather than consumer loans. I have noticed heavy emphasis, for example, on the leasing of capital equipment.
The activities of the corporation, to put it mildly, have been very successful. Among Canadian financial institutions, leaving aside insurance companies, it ranks eleventh in assets and sixth in terms of equity. The following table gives some idea of its place in the Canadian financial world.

Then we come down to the various trust companies and smaller institutions. The years 1974 and 1975 have been very good for IAC. It had net income, (profits) of some $23,336,000 in the year ending December 31, 1974. In the year ended December, 1975, its profits zoomed up to $30,450,000, an increase of some 30 per cent. Dividends paid out jumped from $1.69 a share in 1974 to $2.18 a share in 1975, a healthy jump of some 29 per cent. So IAC is not doing badly for itself as it is presently constituted.
As the IAC people freely admit, IAC, with consolidated assets of well over $2 billion, is Canada's largest sales finance and consumer loan company. If IAC were a chartered bank it would be Canada's sixth bank in terms of equity and eighth in terms of assets. From a humble beginning IAC is already in the major leagues.
IAC has seven subsidiaries. The first is Niagara Finance Company Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary. It is the largest Canadian-owned consumer loan company, with some 260 branches all across Canada, and with some operations in the United Kingdom. It does sales financing and personal loans, which are usually secured through a chattel mortgage.

Capital Funds IAC Ltd., and Capital Funds (IAC Ontario) Ltd. are both wholly owned subsidiaries which deal mostly in commercial loans. Both of these, plus Niagara Finance, can be absorbed virtually whole by the new bank, except for the leasing of capital equipment which is done by the two Capital Funds companies and which is not presently allowed to a bank under the Bank Act.
It is widely assumed, incidentally, that the revision of the Bank Act in 1977 will allow banks to get into leasing of capital equipment since it is a highly lucrative field that is at present being left to other financial institutions. If this is so, then by the time the bank sets up for business this type of business will be eligible to be included also, and can simply be absorbed directly.
When I first heard of this bill I wondered why the banks were not objecting to it. After all, it is not usual for a group of six large corporations which have virtually a monopoly among themselves not to object in such a case. I was puzzled. In my blissful ignorance of business I assumed that the banks would, either publicly or privately, have been opposed to the IAC application. I wondered why there was no opposition. An hon. member over there is pointing in this direction. I assume he means that someone on this side of the House could give an explanation. My suggestion to the hon. member is that he should make his own speech. We would be glad to hear from him rather than have the type of pointing of fingers and verbal objections to which we are so accustomed.
As I said a moment ago, I was puzzled why the banks were not defending their interests and making sure that there was not a new competitor. I was puzzled until it was pointed our to me that, if this bill should pass, IAC in 1976 under its new name Continental Bank of Canada would be involved in business which is not now permitted under the Bank Act, business which the Royal Bank of Canada, the Bank of Montreal, the Imperial Bank of Canada, and the Bank of Nova Scotia are not permitted to transact.
It is obvious from what I have placed on the record in respect of the operation of IAC that this is a very lucrative field of business. Of course the banks would like to have a piece of the action which is now permitted them. Those of us who were here before 1966 and remember the debate which took place at that time-

Mr. Speaker, I wish to complete my remarks simply by saying I am amazed that, on the government side at least, there seems to be a disposition on the part of members, who have much more experience in the business world that I and most if not all members of our party, to support this legislation which will benefit so tremendously one specific corporation, and will do so by a change in the rules which will apply to all the banks which now must follow the rules which are set out clearly and explicitly in the Bank Act. Moreoever, this is being done at a time when we are just one year away from a major revision, if we so desire, of the Bank Act which was passed in 1966.

Mr. Speaker, it is on a very rare occasion that I become involved in a debate dealing with financial institutions. However, at this time I should like to lay before the House my bias in this connection. I have found that banks and trust companies are the least desireble institutions to which an individual, a private person, should go in order to obtain a loan. I have always found, on the contrary, that credit unions are much more co-operative and are much more mindful of the reason why banking, financial institutions, and trust companies exist.
Bill S-30 is designed to establish a new bank which will convert the assets of IAC Limited into its operation. The point of our opposition to this bill and of the amendment we recently placed before the House is that this is a most irregular way of attempting to convert a finance company into a bank. I notice that the company chose first to introduce this bill in the Senate in the hope, quite understandably, it would receive a much more positive reception there because of the number of Senators who have an interest in banks. Indeed the bill was quite speedily approved there.
I think it is important that this House should examine a little more closely the bill which is before us. We should consider the dangerous precedent involved in allowing a finance institution such as this to avoid the carefully thought out provisions and safeguards contained in the Bank Act of Canada. We believe the amendment we suggest should be carefully considered because what we have here is the thin edge of the wedge in subverting the Bank Act which has been set up to protect the people of Canada. speechtext:
I do not want to be distracted by some former adversaries on the football field who know a little bit about the Maritimes, but because of their interest in the Maritimes they will understand why I am rising tonight pursuant to an objection filed under the act protesting the proposal of the Electoral Boundaries Commission for Nova Scotia, and in particular how that proposal affects the riding I have the honour to represent, the historic riding of Annapolis Valley, which the proposal would change.
Our time is rather limited tonight but at the outset I should like to thank the House leaders for mutually agreeing to arrange this time for debate on the last day I could rise in this House to bring a formal objection under the act to the attention of hon. members. I also want to thank the hon. members who joined with me in filing the formal objection and those hon. members who have indicated to me, to amplify the objection, that they are prepared to speak tonight and/or any other time this matter might come before the House.
It might seem rather peculiar to those in the gallery, let alone hon. members opposite and perhaps hon. members on all sides, what is going on here tonight, but the fact is that I am rising at the last stage of the legislative machinery to protest a proposal by the Electoral Boundaries Commission suggesting new boundaries for the riding I represent. I feel very strongly about this. I made representations before the Electoral Boundaries Commission in Halifax when it had

its hearings there, the same as it had its hearings across the country, and there is no doubt that there is a certain quirk in the act whereby, under the law of the land, anything we say tonight is read by the same commissioners who made the proposal. Therefore we have a situation like the original judge and jury deciding whether their verdict was correct, and this does pose difficulties.
I can certainly say to you, Sir, that since this proposal has been laid upon the Table of this House, pursuant to the law of the land, my office has been swamped with letters, petitions, and protests over the proposal to cut the Annapolis Valley in half and join it with other parts of the beautiful province of Nova Scotia.
I want to say at the outset that I have nothing against any part of Nova Scotia. I should like to be the member for any part of it, any part of the Annapolis Valley, any part of the district of Halifax, or anywhere else, but at this point I happen to be the member for the riding called Annapolis Valley.
In my view there are few parts of this country that have such an identity of interest as the Annapolis Valley in generic terms. There is the Niagara Peninsula, but it is being paved and having condominiums built upon it, and its apple orchards and vineyards being ruined. The Okanagan Valley, if you mention the name-

I do not blame the commissioners, but I have been rather involved with the public of Canada in the last six months,

Mr. Speaker, and there is no doubt that there is an alienation factor between the public and the politician-that is me, that is you, that is every member of this House. There is an alienation factor between the public and the elected person because the public wonders what its small voice has to say in something to do with government. What is more basic to government and the law of the land than the ridings from which we come?
I wish I had more time, Mr. Speaker, and I hope I can have it extended with the help of my colleagues before the debate concludes. I hope there will be an opportunity to file a petition that is now being circulated in the Annapolis Valley, with X number of names for the moment. There are already 1,000 to 1,500 names on file, and I suggest in terms of the specific issue there are very few things I have been involved with in the ten years that I have been a member of this House that have produced 1,500 letters or coupons, individually signed and individually written, such as this one protesting the proposal of the commissioners.
I say in all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, that the voice of Canadians from coast to coast, the voice of particular Canadians in my riding who protest this change, has to be heard. It has to be heard more than in just the formal procedures of the electoral boundary commission holding hearings in different parts of Nova Scotia.
I suggest the very fact that the Gazette notice of the hearings was published on July 29, in the middle of summer, did not help generate public interest in the proposal for the new riding. I think the House should look at the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act and make sure that the Gazette notices will never again be published in the middle of summer when Canadians are involved in other things.
I wish the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain, who has such gusto, would contain it when I am speaking about something I know is dear to his heart, that is, the representation of people. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member who just spoke was getting some advice from the member behind him, the hon. member for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell). Interestingly enough she has not made any representation at all and this is going to affect her as much as it is going to affect me. But let us leave that alone, Mr. Speaker.
The fact of the matter is that the Gazette notice was published on July 29 when most Canadians were enjoying vacations. Then under the auspices of the government we had a postal strike that went on for weeks so it was difficult for the public to register objection to the proposal or get in touch with their member.
These are some things which adversely affected the public interest, which kept individual Canadians from raising their collective voice as 2,000 of them have done in these files that I hold. These letters are trying to tell the commissioners that their proposal to cut the Annapolis Valley in half is against geography, against history, against the economy, and against the very community of interests that has made the Annapolis Valley a very valuable part of the fabric of Canada since 1604.
Our problems are different from those of larger areas such as Oshawa, and urban areas that grow overnight, where it is difficult to have a definable community of interests. My area has had that for almost 300 years. But because of the machinations of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, and on the basis of statistics, it is going to be cut in two.
The main interest in many parts of the riding of South Western Nova is fishing, and under the proposal it is suggested that Annapolis Valley will be incorporated into that riding. Historically, geographically, and economically the main occupation of Annapolis Valley is agriculture. You can see a real division of interest right there, Mr. Speaker.
I would be the last one to claim pride of authorship for words of wisdom that I think should be followed. In the submission I filed several months ago with the commission I objected on the basis of history, geography, economy and education to changing the name of the riding to Kings-Hants. After all we want names to mean something in this country.
We have heard much talk of Canadian content. Pierre Berton wrote "The Last Spike", a saga of the Canadian Pacific Railway, because he was interested in Canadian history. You have Peter Newman, who now has a virtual monopoly with Maclean's with the help of the government, trying to foster Canadianism. My hon. friend, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) wears the kilt on the historic days of which he is so proud. We are proud of our history. My part of the country has history coming out of its ears, yet the Electoral Boundaries Commission wants to cut up a district which has been a unit for the past 200 or 300 years.
I appreciate that in older, historically significant regions it is more difficult to make boundary changes. Few communities in Canada have such a community of interest as the Annapolis Valley, the place where European civilization first flourished in this country. After all, western
Electoral Boundaries
civilization first established itself in eastern Canada at Port Royal, in 1604. European civilization flourished there and grew from there.
Not only is the valley a unit historically; it is a unit topographically, educationally, and economically. A long time ago Edmund Burke defined a community of interest in "Reflections on a Revolution in France", page 399, as follows;
Society becomes a partnership between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.

speechtext: We're sad.

subsubtopic: OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
I ask the hon. member to constrain his tears. I know his speech.
My family is from the Annapolis Valley. My good friend, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forre-stall), is from the valley too. We have extensive roots there. Now the place which is one historic unit, the unity of which I consider as my historic birthright, is to be severed, separated, no longer to be known as one riding, Annapolis Valley.

subsubtopic: OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext: Come off it!

subsubtopic: OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
The hon. member does not know what he is talking about. He is oohing and aahing. That is the hot gas socialists produce. What's more, the hon. member is not being sociable.
I know the Electoral Boundaries Commission is sincere. Its members should look at the area not from the viewpoint of statistics but from the much broader viewpoint of community of interest. I say that the valley is a community and, as such, its wishes should be respected. I know that the commission is sensitive about electoral boundaries and splitting regions. You know, it is one thing to divide a community, quite another to define it. Our community has been defined for hundreds of years. Now the commission wants to divide it and make it into two new ridings.
The area has produced at least three Canadian prime ministers. The Secretary of State for External Affairs no doubt has heard of Right Hon. Lorimer Ilsley, who was one of the best ministers of finance we have ever had. He came from the area.

speechtext:
No, Joe, it isn't. The commission cannot ignore deeply rooted traditions. The area is one unit educationally, served by a university attended by between 60 per cent and 70 per cent of students who come from the valley. Why, if this proposal carries, the people in the valley will be divided. How can they ask with one voice for manpower programs which may be necessary, or for OFY grants, if the government continues to give them? The governemnt isn't sure of anything. I do not suppose the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) knows what he will do next. He probably isn't sure if he should shave his beard tonight. That's how unsettled he is.
Why should you divide the region? Why should some students at Acadia University be represented by one member and some students by another, which will happen if you establish the new riding of Kings-Hants?
Think also of what will happen to CFB Greenwood, part of which is in Kings county and the other part in Annapolis. Under this proposal some of the married service personnel living at Middleton will vote in one riding; others at the base will vote in the other. That is preposterous. Greenwood is right on the borderline of the proposed riding. CFB Greenwood, incidentally, is the largest base east of Montreal and the large NATO base in Canada. Why create such problems at the base? Our school systems are also involved in the proposed change.
The two towns affected, Middleton and Bridgetown, are none too happy with the proposed change. The clerk of the town of Middleton wrote me the following letter, a copy of which went to the chief commissioner. It says:
The town of Middleton wishes to make known its views and opinions regarding the proposed federal electoral boundaries changes in the Annapolis Valley.
Although approximately one half of Annapolis county is now included in the Digby-Yarmouth electoral boundaries region, the town feels that should any changes be made in these boundaries, that Annapolis county in its totality, should be included with the Kings-Hants riding.
Annapolis county has traditionally been closely linked with the rest of Annapolis Valley community, not only in its history but in its present economic ties.
The economic mainstay of the Annapolis Valley is agriculture; the mainstay for the Yarmouth-Digby riding is fishing. Should Annapolis county be included in the Yarmouth-Digby riding, the federal representative would then have to be well experienced in agriculture and fishing as well and would, of necessity, have to have close liaison with the other MP representing the valley riding. This condition could cause a great deal of unco-ordination in efforts to assist the agricultural community of the Annapolis Valley as a whole and further complicate the position of the representative were he to try to represent these two economic mainstays in the Annapolis-Digby-Yarmouth region.
For these reasons the town of Middleton feels that rather than change the boundaries to include the Annapolis county with Digby-Yarmouth counties, that the commission should give serious consideration if any change is made at all, to include Annapolis county with the Kings-Hants riding. The town of Middleton wishes that the Annapolis Valley be left intact as one historical and economic entity and that one federal representative for the Valley should speak for the entire Valley community.
I could not agree more with those thoughts and sentiments. They were filed after the representation hearings were held because of the difficulty of summertime and the postal strike.
The mayor of Bridgetown has written to the commissioner. I quote from his letter:
On the 8th of October 1975 our Town Council addressed a letter to Judge Angus MacDonald expressing our dissatisfaction and opposition to the proposed changes in electoral boundaries which would attach all of Annapolis County to the South Nova constituency.
[Mr. Guay (St. Boniface).)
We understand the Nova Scotia commission on electoral boundaries has now submitted its report, which does approve the change noted above, even though there is widespread and strong opposition from this part of the province.
This is the dilemma that faces Canadians because they do not understand the legislative machinery that has to be followed. Quite frankly I hope we have some effect in going through this procedure tonight. The mayor continued:
While not fully aware of the procedure in such instances, we understand that the only recourse now-
Again, this came late in the day because of the summer recess, vacations, and the postal strike.
-is an appeal on the part of a number of elected members of the House of Commons. Just how this is accomplished we do not know, and would welcome advice from you as to what we might do to assure further careful consideration to this very serious and disruptive proposed electoral change.
We recognize that this is a late hour appeal, but at the same time it is due only to the fact that our appeal of October 8, 1975, was not favourably received.
I'm sure you will recognize at once that this request comes from a responsible elected body, and reflects the apprehension and concern of the people of our area.
Without being more specific, it must be quite clear that the proposed change would be both disturbing and disruptive. It follows quite logically too that all possible should be done to retain the harmony and satisfaction which presently prevails.
We urge you to consider this letter as a reasoned and well-considered appeal for further study of a proposal which promises to promote dissatisfaction and disharmony.
Those are submissions from two of the larger towns in the area that is going to be cut back and tied into another constituency, which is undoubtedly tremendous, but one with which they have never been associated in any way whatsoever.
I have a resolution from 17 or 18 Annapolis Valley boards of trade who also protest this move. I have a petition signed by over 2,000 people that I hope to file before this hearing is concluded in this House.
It is very difficult in this formal Chamber to try to relate the serious personal concern and confusion of people who have always been a part of an area and overnight their boundaries are going to be changed. As I said, this is not a new area. For the past 50 years Annapolis Valley has been an electoral unit and this proposal is cutting it up. It does not have to happen.
When I made my representation to the regional commissioner in Halifax, it so happened that Mr. Castonguay was there. He is a very respected Canadian who knows more about the electoral procedure and boundary changes than any other Canadian. In my submission I stated that all of Annapolis County, all of Kings County, and at least half of East Hants, which I now represent, should be in the constituency of Annapolis Valley. In fact, as far as I am concerned, it should be all of Annapolis County, Kings County and Hants County.
My friend who represents East Hants is prepared to speak on my proposal. He will say that East Hants has a community interest with either Truro or Windsor and no community interest with Annapolis Valley. It is not even part of the Annapolis Blossom Festival. It is not related with regard to newspapers or radio. Mr. Castonguay stated that I was the first member to appeal before a commission
March 11, 1976

hearing and advocate taking on more people, rather than less. Mr. Castonguay caught the point completely because in terms of the Annapolis Valley community interest, I or whoever is the member, would serve more people. That is because the community interest is so definable. The interests are similar. To divide Annapolis Valley in two and add a portion to one part, with all respect to the lovely people of East Hants there would not be the same community interest that is historic in the Annapolis Valley. I hope the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) will say a few words.
With the consent of the House, I or another member on my behalf, will file the necessary petitions and formal signatures. This can be done at a later date. However, I plead that statistics not be the determining factor for a constitutency that has been a historic part of the land for 300 years. It is the soul of the Annapolis Valley that I plead for in terms of electoral representation rather than just the cold, formal statistics that are applied to determining electoral boundaries. There is now a definable boundary in terms of Annapolis Valley. I do not understand why the commission should use statistics to cut it in half.

subsubtopic: OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always nice to support a colleague and have so much gratuitous advice thrown across the floor from people who have forsaken the maritime way and gone to other places, but still have the interests of the maritimes at heart.
My purpose in rising is to suggest a way out of the dilemma posed by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan). I rarely rise in this place to scold, but only when I think of some kind of remedy that might or might not be applied, or at least should be considered. It is my purpose to follow that sort of course this evening.
I do not know whether hon. members realize it or not, members like the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) would realize it, but the hon. member for Annapolis Valley is telling it exactly as it is. There has developed a rather explosive situation in Nova Scotia in connection with the redistribution of seats.
Knowing the people who sat on the commission I must say I thought that, by and large, they did an excellent job. Mr. Justice Angus MacDonald has been a friend and associate of mine for years and years. His father was the distinguished premier of Nova Scotia for years back. Knowing him and others who sat on the commission, they did the best they could. The fact is, however, that once in a while one is allowed to blunder. OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is nice to see us going from one end of the country to the other and eliminating most of the stuff in the middle for a change. It is my privilege tonight to speak on behalf of a couple of other members from British Columbia who happen to be away from this House on very important business, namely, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) and the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt).
The points I wish to make touch on three types of characteristics: geographical, political and demographic. Specifically I wish to inform you that the Creston Valley area of the present day riding of Kootenay West should not be redistributed into the new riding of Kootenay East, and that the Christina Lake area should remain in Okanagan Boundary rather than be added to Kootenay West. The hon. member for Kootenay West, who has asked me to speak on his behalf in his absence, states that he would like to make it absolutely clear at the outset that he personally has no objections to serving and representing the Christina Lake area; indeed he has many friends in that community. None the less, he does not feel it to be fair to either the people of Christina Lake or of Creston or even of Trout Lake that the proposed redistribution take place.
Geographically speaking, the Creston Valley area forms a natural boundary for the southeastern limits of Kootenay West, as does the Rossland range of mountains in the southwest, and as do the Monashees on the north end of the Arrow Lakes. By contrast, Christina Lake and its

March 11, 1976
Electoral Boundaries
environs are at the base of a natural obstruction, namely, a high mountain pass known as the Blueberry-Paulson, and does not geographically belong to the natural boundaries of present day Kootenay West.
In effect what the proposed redistribution does is oblige the member for Kootenay West to travel over an additional mountain pass, which in winter is not only time consuming but also difficult and hazardous. Anyone who has lived in the Kootenays for a winter will know that eastern Canada's snowfalls are minor compared to those in his area. There is no permanent habitation along the 60 odd miles of this pass. In order to cover the east side of Kootenay Lake in the redistributed riding, the hon. member would have two choices before him. He can take the ferry at the north end of the lake and, on reaching the east side, swing 40 miles south. This ferry runs once every 45 minutes, but is frequently delayed in winter due to weather, and in summer due to heavy tourist traffic. Or he could travel over the Salmo-Creston Skyway through what would become his former riding and then drive approximately 40 miles north. Either way, he is severely inconvenienced.
Further to this, should it prove impossible to persuade the commission to leave Creston in Kootenay West, surely they can leave the north end of Kootenay Lake in his riding. This would be an improvement in that it is far easier to travel the few extra miles to this remote part of his riding, a part which shares in the concerns of Kootenay West as it now exists, than to service the Christina Lake area.
Politically speaking he would like to draw the commission's attention to the fact that two community bodies which are representative of a cross-section of the people in the Creston area have rejected any inclusion of Creston into the new Kootenay East riding. The Creston Chamber of Commerce spoke against the proposed redistribution and, as well, the Creston Town Council unanimously voted to reject the proposed change. The stand taken by these two bodies is understandable in light of the fact that prior to 1952 Creston was in the riding of Kootenay East and was moved back to Kootenay West in 1965. Another move back to Kootenay East would only confirm the feeling of the local populace that their fate is to be a political football approximately once every 10 to 15 years, serving only to satisfy the whims of redistribution and the numerical population needs of redistribution. He would suggest to members of the commission that this is totally unnecessary in light of the following demographic considerations.
In November of 1974 the British Columbia Research Council issued a report entitled "Population Projection" wherein it outlined the following statistics. In the regional district of Kootenay Boundary in 1974 the population was 31,407; the projection for 1980 is 30,763. In the central Kootenay area in 1974 the population was 44,670; the projection for 1980 is 47,265. In Columbia Shuswap the population in 1974 was 30,811; the projection for 1980 is 40,647. In East Kootenay the population in 1974 was 39,735; the projection for 1980 is 52,475.
The first two regional districts, corresponding roughly to the land area of Kootenay West, will experience approximately 7.8 per cent growth by 1980. The second two regional districts, corresponding almost exactly to the new riding of Kootenay East, will experience a 63.3 per cent growth by

1980. Even if we tend to be pessimistic about future economic growth, Kootenay East will more than make up for the 5,000 or so constituents it will not get if Kootenay East keeps its present proportions.
It is pertinent to note in this connection the statement by Premier Bennett of British Columbia that coal is going to play a major part in the provincial economy and that it is going to be a part of the new economic prosperity. The riding of Kootenay East encompasses the largest and most development-ready coal mining area in all of British Columbia. At the rates predicted by the British Columbia Research Council, Kootenay East will, in a matter of 4.8 years, have gained about 5,000 people, already sufficient to make the addition of Creston superfluous. It is therefore highly likely that after the next census Creston will once again be redistributed back to Kootenay West.
The hon. member would also like to point out that economic trading patterns presently exist between Creston, Nelson, and Trail, rather than between Creston and Cranbrook. Similarly, the people of Christina Lake do their trading mainly with Grand Forks. It is not appropriate or fair to the people of Christina Lake that the economic concerns of Christina Lake be included in those of Kootenay West, just as it is not appropriate or fair that the economic concerns of Creston be included in those of Kootenay East, an area whose economic concerns differ widely from those encountered in Kootenay West.
Finally the hon. member would like to make a point about the peculiar manner in which the commission has drawn the boundaries in his present riding across areas that are virtually uninhabited the year round, presumably in the name of fair redistribution. He asks that you take note of the fact that the commission has drawn a line through hundreds of square miles of Kootenay West in an area bounding the Salmo-Creston Skyway, the area north of Creston, and the area bounding Trout Lake and Upper Arrow Lake. It is inconceivable to him how the mere addition of hundreds of square miles of bush can be justification for the commission's supposed aim of fair apportionment of constituents to every member's riding.
Did the commission find any great and pressing concerns in these areas of forests, high mountain peaks, and surging creeks which would cause it to put them into either Kootenay East or Okanagan North? If so, the hon. member is most anxious to hear about them. He does not think it too much to ask that at least those portions which play no part in this population redistribution be left in Kootenay West since these areas are ones of present and future environmental, economic, and other concerns to those constituents left in Kootenay West after redistribution.
In any case the hon. member would like to demand from the commission a full explanation as to why it insisted on such a move. Perhaps such an explanation will remove the lingering doubts in his mind, and in the minds of other members of parliament who have suffered the same fate as he, as to whether or not the commission's work is serious 100 per cent of the time, or whether it redistributes ridings in a manner akin to shuffleboard.
I should like to talk now about some ridings on the lower mainland of British Columbia. I propose that the electoral
March 11, 1976

district of Burnaby-New Westminster be formed by joining that section of the proposed Burnaby riding which is west of Sperling Avenue and Kingsway to the city of New Westminster. An electoral district of Burnaby-Capitol Hill can be formed by joining the Capitol Hill district to the section of the proposed Burnaby riding which is east of Sperling and the Kingsway. An electoral district of Coquitlam, Port Coquitlam and Port Moody can be formed by joining these three districts.
The following reasons are urged for my proposals: Capitol Hill, proposed now as part of North Vancouver-Burna-by, should be electorally associated with Burnaby. Geographically being separated from the rest of its proposed constituency by Burrard Inlet, the residents of Capitol Hill have little or no association with North Vancouver. Consider the separation, the inconvenience; there is not even a bridge to the North Vancouver district within the Capitol Hill section, therefore all social and commercial relations flow south connecting Capitol Hill easily with Burnaby. Culturally and socio-economically, the Capitol Hill quarter is associated with Burnaby and not with North Vancouver.
It is obvious that the interests and concerns of Capitol Hill residents are similar to those of Burnaby, while in an enlarged North Vancouver-Burnaby electoral district they will be an unrepresented minority. In this area I feel sympathy for the present member for New Westminster because the riding I now represent, Burnaby-Richmond-Delta, has a part of Burnaby that is totally separated from Richmond-Delta. From either end of my riding I have to drive about ten miles through the ridings of a couple of other members to get to the rest of my riding in Burnaby. From the Delta end of my constituency I have to drive through the ridings of other members and across a bridge to get to the other section of my riding. The people living in that area of Burnaby really have no relation with those living in Richmond and Delta which are brand new areas, growing fast, whereas Burnaby has been there for much longer.
That has been a hardship for this member mainly because of the distance one has to drive around there and because of the disassociation, not being next door neighbours. I would have hoped the commission, when drawing up these boundaries, would have given more attention to these factors because the people in Capitol Hill, who will now have a representative who most likely will be on the north shore, will not even have a bridge-they will have to drive through the ridings of other members to get to the rest of the area of the riding they will be associated with. I can't understand the members of the commission when they draw things up like this because certainly some of the members of that commission know British Columbia better than would seem from the lines that are on the maps.
The western section of the proposed Burnaby riding should be joined to the city of New Westminster since the historic, commercial, and social relationships of a large part of that section have been with the city of New Westminster. Again the hon. member is pointing out that people who are socially and economically in the same area should be left in the same area.
Coquitlam should be in the same riding as Port Coquitlam and Port Moody. All are new suburbs, all are within the same school district, and all have similar socio-econom-

ic mixes. By putting those areas together, Coquitlam would then become the centre of a major riding, and this again would serve the people of that area much better.
Now that I have made some comments for the member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Kootenay West I might make some on my own area and also on the province in general. I have attended all the public hearings and a number of the meetings which have been held. I remember the debates in the last parliament when redistribution got shot down, much to my dismay because of the fact that I represent one of the largest ridings in the country, in excess of 200,000 people. I am disturbed that once again I have to go back to an election with the same large group of people which is awfully tough to represent, especially when you look at members from Newfoundland and the smaller provinces who have only 30,000 electors. You then think it would be nice if you could get your riding down to the same size and maybe give the people a little more service.

speechtext: How many blocks is it?

subtopic: OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I hear someone down there yelling "How many blocks is it?" Mine is also a large riding geographically. Certainly in the rush hour I could not drive around my riding in seven hours the way the traffic is blocked up at tunnels and bridges. Some of the members who represent rural areas must think it would be awfully nice to represent an urban area, but they do not realize that people disappear into their cars in the morning and do not come back until late at night. It is not always that easy. Besides, the people in the urban areas tend to become more involved in politics.
The point I am making is that British Columbia was alloted only five new seats in the redistribution and the way I heard some of the members talk in the House it was great we were getting so many. But the main error of the whole redistribution setup is that it was taken on the basis of a census which was so old. If it had been based on the 1971 census British Columbia would have qualified for a lot more seats than five. Members might say that this would apply to every other area, but no province in this country has shown the growth rate of British Columbia.
We are the fastest growing province in the country and the reason is obvious to everyone who lives there. The hon. member who is speaking has lived in two eastern provinces; he happened to be born down here and has lived in two of the western provinces, but the province of British Columbia seems to have nicer weather which attracts a lot of people from this area to live there, and maybe that is why our growth rate is so great. Certainly after this redistribution, even if it takes place within a very short period of time, most of the members from British Columbia will represent constituencies with far more people in them than members in other parts of the country. I think this is a shame.
We should look toward a system of redistribution which would redistribute the ridings on the basis of population figures much more up to date than those we are using. I was looking at the map, and looking at the numbers of people I am going to have in my riding, and I was amazed to find that the figure is roughly 83,000-that is the number the commission says will be in the new riding of

March 11, 1976
Electoral Boundaries
Richmond-South Delta. Well, there are already in excess of
90.000	people in the Richmond area alone, and in excess of
30.000	in the South Delta area. So the minimum population by the time redistribution comes in will give me at least
120.000	constituents. This is a considerable number to represent.
The way they split up my riding, I cannot complain. After saying there are so many people to look after, I am very pleased that those people in the Burnaby area will be going into a riding represented for the first time. Right now there is no one member who represents Burnaby. My riding is Burnaby-Richmond-Delta and there is a member on the other side of the House who represents Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Raines), but there is no member who represents Burnaby only. That is the one good thing this commission has brought out after recommendations from members on both sides of the House, that Burnaby should have one member to represent the area, one of our larger municipalities. I am very happy, and I am sure the people of Burnaby South, who I have been proud to represent in two elections and who in the last election, in every poll, voted for me with over 50 per cent of the vote, will be pleased that they will now be represented by a member who lives in Burnaby, althouth I am sure they feel they are well represented, and have been, not only by this member but by other members in the past who, by the way, mostly all lived in the Richmond or Delta area.
As far as Richmond goes, those people will still have a member of parliament to represent them, and that member will only have to represent South Delta as well as Richmond I still feel that if the redistribution were carried out on a more up to date basis the community of Richmond should have a member of parliament of its own. A community with a population in excess of 90,000 should not have to share its member of parliament with another community in the area, especially when one considers the size of some other ridings in the country.
When it comes to the Delta area I shall be losing the North Delta area to a riding that will be called North Delta-Surrey-White Rock. That might fit well together geographically, but again it is a shame because Delta encompasses three distinct communities. It is the southeas-ternmost part of the mainland of Canada, it borders on the United States, and it is called the sun capital of Canada. This area receives less rain and more sunshine than anywhere else in the country. It is a shame this area has to be split in half through redistribution when it has in excess of
65.000	to 70,000 people and could qualify in most regions of the country as a riding in its own right.
I must say in all fairness that the commissioners had to take into consideration the old census. This is the only way they could do it and we will have to go along with it. However, I am looking forward to the day that Delta will be a riding on its own. I am sure it will reach that point at the next redistribution after this.
I hope that as soon as this redistribution is completed the House will set up a committee to review and redistribute seats. I know that the Committee on Privileges and Elections is looking into the area of permanent voters' lists and so on, which ought to speed up many of those things and

perhaps make us look a little more professional to the people of Canada than we do at the present time when we try to redistribute our seats. Mr. Speaker, that is about all I have to say about redistribution. I thank the House for listening to my remarks about my area, the area of the hon. member for Kootenay West, and that of the hon. member for New Westminster.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take a few minutes tonight to speak about the redistribution in British Columbia, and more specifically in my constituency of Kamloops-Cariboo. By and large the Commission has done a fantastic job in the province of British Columbia. Many of us are concerned about the rapid growth in the province. We are very happy to see that finally we are to be allocated five new constituencies. My representation was that we should have six new constituencies, but five is pretty close.
British Columbia has been one of the most rapid growth provinces in the country. Five new seats reflect this new growth. This growth has been all over. It is in the lower mainland and also in the upper interior in places such as Prince George, Kamloops, Kelowna, and Penticton. These cities have grown extremely rapidly. I want to congratulate the commission for having taken all these factors into consideration.
As I said before, the commission really has done a pretty fantastic job in British Columbia. Some pretty strong representations have been made to me from the city of Merritt. Hearings were held in Kamloops at which presentations were made. There was one presentation by the Shulus Indian Band on behalf of the Indians in that part of the constituency, and another by the Merritt Chamber of Commerce. These people were extremely concerned about the city of Merritt no longer being included in a constituency with Kamloops.
The old constituency of Kamloops-Cariboo had about
140,000	people. It covered an area of about 25,000 square miles. There were some anomalies in the old distribution. It was necessary to try to fit people into some areas which were very large. In some instances there was no relationship between one area and the other in respect of, for instance, Kamloops and Quesnel. When the last redistribution took place there was much concern that Quesnel, so many miles away from Kamloops, had to be in the same constituency. In any event it all worked out. After all the shouting was over it was fantastic for me to represent Kamloops-Cariboo along with the city of Quesnel.
I want to say I hope the commission will look again at the matter of including Merritt with Kamloops in a constituency. In the redistribution it is now with Okanagan-Similkameen. Merritt really has no connection with the area of Okanagan-Similkameen except perhaps with Princeton. It has no affinity with Penticton or the Okanagan part of British Columbia. The real connection of Merritt is with Kamloops. Its connection with Kamloops is in such areas as the newspapers. The people in Merritt read the Daily Sentinel and the Kamloops News. Many people in Kamloops also read the Merritt Herald and the Merrittonian and so on. There is a natural connection also through television and radio. Radio Station CHNL Kamloops has an outlet in Merritt and Princeton as well as in Clearwater
March 11, 1976

which is up the North River. The same thing applies to the mining industry and the forest industry.
With these few comments may I say, on behalf of the people of Merritt, that I hope I have registered with the commission their concern so that the commission may take another look at the situation in an effort to ensure that the Merritt-Quilchena area will be included with Kamloops where they want it to be, and with which there is a natural connection geographically, socially, and economically.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the commissioners for the good job they have done in the basic redistribution of the ridings in British Columbia. They do not have an easy job in the mountainous area of British Columbia. It really is not too easy to get everybody in exactly the areas where they would like to be. I should also say that probably they recognized at the outset that the city of Merritt needed some really good representation. Perhaps that is the reason why they included that city in the new riding of Okana-gan-Similkameen. I think I must agree with the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) that the basic economic community is joined to the city of Kamloops and that area more than it is to the rest of the new riding that is being created, Okanagan-Similkameen. So I would think that even though the commissioners wanted to get better representation for the people there, the area really should be included in the Kamloops areas.
Also in the redistribution the new riding is called Okanagan-Similkameen. The name of the riding now is Okanagan Boundary and the only difference between Okanagan Boundary and what we would have is the inclusion of the city of Merritt at the north western extremity and the exclusion of the small community of Christina Lake in the southeastern boundary, and then dividing it up into another riding which would include Kelowna, Vernon and Enderby. Actually we are getting in the very high growth area, bearing in mind that the riding of Okanagan Boundary has the third largest population in British Columbia, and that takes in all the ridings in the area, including Vancouver. It is a big riding with a large population.
You might get many complaints from city ridings, but I know that in most of them you can cover the whole area on a bicycle. There is no way that you can do that in a riding such as Okanagan Boundary. Many of the city ridings in Canada have small populations, such as Vancouver East and Vancouver-Kingsway. They contain not much more than half of the population of the riding of Okanagan Boundary.
I also agree with the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Brisco) that Christina Lake should not be included in the riding of Kootenay West. There is a mountain range between the city of Castlegar and Christina Lake. In May of 1974 when I went over to the nomination meeting of the hon. member who now sits for Kootenay West-I hope I did a little bit to help him get here-I came back that evening over the mountain range, with mountains on both sides of the highway covered with snow, and on the way I encountered a bear and her cub. The bear cub had just been born up high on the mountain range which was
Electoral Boundaries
covered with snow, and this was in May. This is the kind of thing we are talking about in British Columbia and these are the kinds of roads we have to travel on in these areas.
Christina Lake is a community which the CRTC and CBC do not consider as having a sufficiently large population to qualify for television coverage under the accelerated program, although there are more than 500 people living there. I believe they went back to the 1971 census in making their decision to exclude that community, a community which is cut off by a mountain range which, at the best of times, is hazardous to cross. Yet the commissioners have decided to include it in the riding of Kootenay West. These people are only seven miles away from the city of Grand Forks. Christina Lake was at one time a resort. Now it is one of the better places in which to live in Canada, as is most of the area that I represent. Many people from all over Canada come to live there. Even a relative of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae) lives there. These are the type of people who move in from all over Canada to live in this community. That is why it is growing so fast.
I think that more study should be devoted to this matter of excluding a community such as Christina Lake and putting it into the riding of Kootenay West, and also including in the riding a community such as Merritt which is closely connected with the city of Kamloops.
I know this has not been an easy task and I would not like to see any of these representations upset the designation given by the commissioners because, as I said at the outset, it is not at all easy to designate ridings in this type of mountainous area. When you consider any interior riding such as mine, with a population which is so much greater than ridings in the great metropolis of Vancouver, you realize that there is an inequality there and that to represent these people properly we must have more seats in the area.
I agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) when he says we are not overjoyed at receiving five new seats in British Columbia. All we received were five new seats in British Columbia. When you compare that with ridings in other areas of Canada such as in the Atlantic provinces, in Quebec, and in many parts of Ontario, you find that we are not getting our just due in British Columbia. More seats should have been given to us. When I look at the redistribution in Ontario I see that ridings in the south and central area of Ontario have a smaller population than some of the great spread-out ridings in British Columbia. I do not understand why we should not get more seats.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. In the very brief time I have I should like to make only two points, and that will take about all the time I have.
One can hardly be too critical of redistribution which in a sense does what I suggested it should do, which is to create two Kootenay and two Okanagan seats, as it was historically. However, an examination of the map shows that it has not really solved some of the problems which existed previously. The large size of Okanagan-Kootenay has been a difficulty to overcome, for any hon. member representing that area, and yet if we look at the proposed Kootenay East, it reaches into north Okanagan on the one end and west Kootenay on the other, and carries for whoever represents it in the future parliament the same difficulties which exist in Okanagan-Kootenay today.
The distances will be tremendous, and if one looks at the Okanagan side of it one sees that north Okanagan has been divided three ways, whereas it was divided two ways before. The Shuswap Sicamous area has been included with Kamloops. It is a great reaching over for that area, so I hope the redistribution commission will consider what it has done because it could have been done differently if the Kootenays hhd been regarded as Kootenays and given two seats. If the whole Okanagan had been treated as a unit and divided into two, a more sensible redistribution would have been made.
