subtopic: OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING ALBERTA
OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we move eastward into the province of Alberta I think even the most solidly entrenched member of parliament would agree that the process whereby riding boundaries are regularly re-evaluated is desirable and necessary in order to ensure adequate representation to fast growing ares and to reflect the experience of those who have been elected to represent a given district. Accepting as we do the necessity, and indeed, the value of redistribution, changes in the province of Alberta must be made with a minimum of major surgery on constituency boundaries except where we must repair anomalies which were introduced in prior redistributions. With respect, I find that some changes in the electoral map which the commission has proposed this time are unacceptable.
As the commission should be aware, the provisions of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act permit certain considerations to influence the delineation of each riding, namely, special geographical considerations, including particularly the sparsity, density or relative rate of growth of various regions of the province, the accessibility of such regions or the shape and size thereof, and any special community or diversity of interests of the inhabitants of various regions of the province.
The tolerance of 25 per cent in either direction from the established quota for each province was written into the act to benefit rural areas. This was much discussed at the time of the last distribution. I know a number of my colleagues will be bringing this point up again tonight. This is to allow rural constituencies to retain their distinctive character and to continue to exist within a representable framework even if, as a result, their population is substantially on the low side of the deviation permitted. I contend that in some respect the commission has ignored these provisions and the intent of the framers of the act.
With specific reference to my riding of Wetaskiwin I cannot comprehend why the commission found it more reasonable to carve out the commuter area south west of Edmonton and move it into the Yellowhead riding. Surely the commuter towns of Spruce Grove, Stony Plain and Winterburn-and the acreages which are adjacent-should not have been taken out of Wetaskiwin because they have much more in common with the suburban area communities of Devon, Leduc and New Sarepta, the demographic interests of which are more urban oriented than that of the large area of Yellowhead where the primary occupations are lumbering, mining, tourism, and agriculture.
Stony Plain, Spruce Grove and Winterburn are situated in an agricultural area dominated principally by hobby and dairy farms, a characteristic similar to that of the Leduc-Devon area. Wetaskiwin is made up of a rich agricultural area with largely a preponderance of dairy farming and other cereal crop farming. It is surrounded by large towns which service that area, along with the commuter area which is south and west of Edmonton.
March 11, 1976

Growth and growth patterns come into this picture as well. The towns of Spruce Grove, Stony Plain, Devon and Leduc have all experienced rapid growth which has virtually doubled their populations over the past few years. Without becoming urbanized these communities will more and more attract light mobile industry which does not need to be located within the city, but which does need to be close to its facilities and transport routes. The employees of these industries, as well as those who commute to and from Edmonton, have special needs and interests. These individuals, along with the specialized farmers, constitute the two readily identifiable and not incompatible populations of the riding. To extract a large group of persons, some 6,000, from this territory and place them in a constituency where the terrain, working pattern and orientation are totally dissimilar to the riding in which they are presently located is contrary to the sense, spirit and letter of the act.
The accomplishment of what has been done is to make Yellowhead riding 71,000 people and the Wetaskiwin riding 64,900 instead of the reverse as it was on the pre-public hearing map of Wetaskiwin, which was 71,700, and the Yellowhead riding 64,044. In our motion in section 8 we suggest that the commission has not established the rationale of the decision to limit the urban city ridings at the boundary limits of the cities of Edmonton and Calgary in order to eliminate a possible urban domination of the adjacent rural populations. It then immediately reversed itself in its designation of adjacent constituencies where the rural populations are entirely dominated by those of suburban communities, the demographic interests of which are solely urban orientated.
The commission decided to limit the urban city ridings at the boundary limits of the cities of Edmonton and Calgary. How can it then justify its delineation of boundaries where, quite obviously, the rural population will be entirely dominated by the suburban communities whose democratic interests are wholly urban orientated? Again I must refer to the Wetaskiwin-Yellowhead situation. The density of the urban-orientated population concentrated in the commuter towns of Spruce Grove, Stony Plain and Winterburn and surrounding acreage, is not comparable to the population dispersal in the farmland and national park area to the west of this region. There is a disparity, and the denser populated region will almost certainly be the dominating influence in the proposed Yellowhead riding.
The situation in which any member representing Yellowhead constituency will find himself cannot be overlooked in the examination of the proposed electoral boundaries. It is entirely conceivable that this individual will be placed in a position where he cannot adequately pursue and forward the interests of agriculture, natural resources, tourism, and the urban commuters in the eastern part of his constituency. The emphasis attached to tourism and the urgency of the development of our natural resources may well overshadow the concerns of the Edmonton oriented suburban group.
Indeed the issues and problems of Jasper National Park and the town of Jasper alone are quite complex. The interests and goals of individuals living in the present Rocky Mountain constituency are peculiar to that area
Electoral Boundaries
alone and demand the full and individual attention of their member of parliament. Will that member be able to represent adequately the divergent interests of the socio-economic composition of both the eastern and western parts of the proposed electoral district?
Since the electoral system is for the primary benefit of the electorate, constituency boundaries must be easily defined and readily identifiable by the constituency population. Riding units should be cohesive and possess as great a common community interest as possible, recognizing working patterns, marketing areas, and demographic factors.
A constituency deserves and should expect the close attention of its member; by this I mean his intimate knowledge of its communities, people, and particular problems, and his regular personal contact throughout that riding. Rural areas generally have been deprived of representation equal to that of urban areas simply because of the distance factor. Because of the increasing difficulty involved in representing a rural constituency, in particular the distance a representative must travel, it is reasonable to expect a rural riding to have a smaller population than an urban riding which is much easier to service.
In the case of the change being made to the Wetaskiwin and Yellowhead constituencies I submit that it would be much easier for the member from Wetaskiwin to serve some 6,000 people living in the commuter towns just outside of Edmonton. The member for Yellowhead, who already has a riding almost three times the size, would be much freer to serve his much larger, more sparsely settled riding than at present. The fact that the urban-orientated area has now entered into a slower expansion era and must now catch up with services such as sewer, water, health and recreational facilities, should not concern the commissioners with regard to projected growth in the area.
Even though the river is a natural boundary, the fifth meridian that was used prior to public hearings adequately divides the commuter area from the other demographic region. This area is used to being in the constituency of Wetaskiwin; it has been there for the past ten years.
I must complain about the fact that no reasons were given for the change from the pre-public hearings to the after public hearings maps. The people in the area extracted from Wetaskiwin and placed in Yellowhead constituency were extremely surprised by the move. They submitted no briefs to the public hearings because they were satisfied with the original delineation. In fact I believe that only one brief was submitted from that area and it was in support of the boundaries as they were then drawn.
I must voice my frustration, and the frustration of some of my colleagues, with the fact that the commissioners did not cite reasons for making changes. The whole burden for launching an attack lies upon the shoulders of the general populace of the area, the members of parliament, and interested organizations. The commissioners in turn never are required to justify their decisions. How are individuals supposed to understand why they have suddenly, for no seemingly apparent reason, been pulled out of one constituency and thrust into another?
At the present time Alberta has 19 seats in the House of Commons, seven of which are totally urban and 12 of

March 11, 1976
Electoral Boundaries
which are rural. With the new proposed boundaries the province will gain two seats. The urban-rural breakdown will be ten to 11. In other words one rural constituency will be lost, therefore making all rural ridings larger than at present. While we recognize that a reasonable effort has been made to delineate boundaries on the east-west line rather than on the pattern as it was before on the north-south boundary, making the riding of Rocky Mountain House very large and hard to represent, we must still complain to the commissioners about the size of the rural constituencies.
I realize that the task of the commission is an extremely difficult one. It is no simple matter to undertake to draw lines on maps, and regardless of where the boundaries are drawn some people will, of course, complain. Admittedly many of the inadequacies of the last redistribution have been rectified. However, I must in conclusion re-emphasize that we now have something new in Alberta since the distribution of 1961, and that is the commuter acreage areas around the two large cities of Edmonton and Calgary. This recent development was taken into consideration and recognized when the boundaries were drawn on the pre-hearing map. The riding of Pembina encompassed the commuter population to the north and east of Edmonton, and Wetaskiwin the towns to the south and west of Edmonton. In the recent map, for unknown reasons, this has been changed.
The danger of dominance of thicker density populated areas over more sparsely populated regions should not be underestimated in deciding upon boundary lines. This can and will create very real and serious problems for constituents and members of parliament. We must recommend in all sincerity that the commission reflect upon these objections and recommendations and reconsider its decision.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO COMMISSION'S REPORT RESPECTING ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as an opening comment in this debate about the new proposals for the Alberta redistribution of federal seats I should like to say it is really much better than the previous attempt in 1973. Of course that one never became operative. This one is much better for my Medicine Hat federal riding.
I would go on to say that, if the only criteria for change were to increase both area and population, then the new proposal that we are discussing tonight for my Medicine Hat riding is both fair and proper as it accomplishes this with the least disruption. It extends the northwest corner and the north side to include the town of Brooks and Bassano and those areas up to the Red Deer River.
I agree with point No. 5 on the objection's statement, which reads:
The commission has failed to take into consideration the size of some of the rural constituencies it has created, and the difficulty involved in representing an area that large. Although Alberta's representation has increased from 19 to 21, three of these go to Kdmonton and Calgary, so that rural Alberta loses one seat.
I suggest sincerely that the 25 per cent variation rule has not been used sufficiently in large, rural constituencies such as Medicine Hat. I am well aware of the principle of representation by population and the specific reference to this principle in the Canada Gazette edition of February 21, 1973, outlining Alberta's federal redistribution and later

references for Alberta. However, I seriously ask this question: is it right and proper that Calgary and Edmonton, with 52 per cent of our provincial population-that figure was used in the proposal-should have almost as many seats as all the remaining cities and towns and, most important, the entire rural areas combined? My answer of course is that the proposed new electoral boundaries are inequitable and ignore the well founded and continuing importance of agriculture and of rural cities, towns, and villages, to our total Alberta economy.
There is now reasonable agreement by governments that the present trends to large super cities should be altered in favour of population and industry dispersal policies. I cannot argue that the "rep-by-pop" principle is unfair when population only is considered; but in view of static or even shrinking rural populations over vast areas we must surely recognize that crowded city living is not in itself justification for over representation in our large cities. Our shrinking rural populations have been due to a vastly increased size of farms brought on by modern agricultural technology and the need for production efficiency. There are now clear signs that the exodus from rural areas may be ending, and in Alberta new provincial policies are being introduced to point out once more that rural industry and living should indeed be considered and encouraged.
The question of enlarging the number of seats in our House of Commons has now achieved some reality. Passage of time and Canadian population growth will make still further enlargement necessary. When this point in our history does arrive I, for one, sincerely hope that these lessons in economic and political disparity, together with the development of our north, will not be sacrificed completely to the cold analytical approach of a purely academic "rep-by-pop" system.
While I have been a member of parliament for only three and a half years I am already acutely aware of the physical problems in properly representing the Medicine Hat federal constituency. It is almost 300 miles by road from Empress, in the northeast corner, to the opposite corner on the U.S. border southwest of Lethbridge. One half of the present population resides in Medicine Hat and Redcliff. The other half includes all the remaining towns and rural residents. With the obvious requirements for House attendance, regular weekend constituency visits are impossible. Travelling schedules from Ottawa to Medicine Hat are such that it takes me much longer to travel from Calgary to my home than from Ottawa to Calgary. A Friday afternoon to Monday noon week end away from Ottawa nets me only about 24 hours in my constituency. I have partially resolved this problem with a constituency office in the city of Medicine Hat. It is run by a very competent secretary five days a week. The proposed new Medicine Hat boundaries will still further aggravate these physical problems, due to a larger area and a larger proportion of the population coming from rural towns and strictly rural areas.
May I make some appropriate comments about the new areas to be added to my riding? I am genuinely pleased to see the addition to my riding to the intensive irrigation districts adjacent to Brooks and Bassano. These regions are surely among the most extensively developed irrigation communities in Alberta, which of course means in all

Canada. This means that my Medicine Hat riding would include nearly all of the intensive irrigation areas of Alberta and, therefore, of Canada. The beautiful towns of Brooks and Bassano are really the products of 70 years of progressive irrigation. The growth of trees, orchards, lawns and shrubs is a joy to behold after one has travelled across the dry land prairies.
I would be remiss in my duty if I did not refer to the new addition across the north side of Medicine Hat riding, that area adjacent to the Red Deer river, east to the Saskatchewan border. This addition contains some of the finest ranch lands in Alberta's short grass, chinook country. It also contains the historic and scenic Dinosaur Park and Bad Lands along the Red Deer River. I also point out that the well known Suffield military reserve of some 1,000 square miles, about which I have been so concerned this last month, will now be totally within Medicine Hat riding.
While I am deeply disturbed and concerned about the physical aspects of representing an ever increasing rural constituency, and although I worry about the dwindling voice of agriculture in this parliament, I am genuinely pleased at the prospect of representing these new additions to my Medicine Hat riding.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate is one step in what has turned out to be a very long process of arriving at new maps for redistributing the electoral districts of Canada from which the members of this House are elected.
The House of course knows that according to the old act the redistribution was to occur as soon as practicable after the 1971 census. This procedure caused new maps to be presented early in 1973, which was in the midst of the term of a minority government. I think it is fair to say that in addition to the reasons given, namely, that the previous act was not truly satisfactory, the fact that with a minority government an election could occur at almost any time had a lot to do with causing members of the House to respond favourably to the suggestion that redistribution be set aside and that a new method be found for deciding upon the electoral districts in the provinces of Canada.
I might say that in terms of my own constituency of Calgary Centre the 1973 map was not that great. It was not that suitable. Basically, it was cutting off one third of the existing constituency of Calgary Centre and adding the equivalent amount of population and geography from other constituencies, but in a manner which dissected existing communities and associated people together who really did not have a common community of interest.
As a result of this decision to set aside redistribution, the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections was presented with a reference from the House and a proposal from the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) on how a new House might be constituted and how the electoral district maps might be decided upon.
I might say in passing that that proposal for deciding upon the basis of the new House did not meet with my approval for the simple reason that it called for an increase in the size of the House. I do not think that would contribute to more efficient conduct of the House of Commons or of the Government of Canada.
As a result of a process of debate and discussion this new procedure was decided upon. It was very similar, except for the number of seats allocated per province, to the old procedure in that an "independent commission" was to be established in each province with a mandate for deciding upon the electoral districts within each province, based roughly on the concept that each electoral district should have an equal number of electors within it.
There were a couple of changes made. One change in particular was unfortunate. The change was that the commissions could no longer take into account trends but rather should be restricted to the data available from the

March 11, 1976
Electoral Boundaries
most recent biennial census. As a result of that we had a situation in Alberta where the constituencies very rigorously followed the act, as is most proper, and therefore the commission cannot be faulted, but that resulted in some anomalies that, although not severe now, will be severe in the near future because of growth patterns within the existing cities. One possible consequence was talked about by my colleague, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schelienberger).
As I understand the commissions will have the benefit of this debate, I must state that the commission in the province of Alberta produced a map in 1975 that was a considerable improvement over the map produced in 1973. It was not perfection, and that is a subjective thing, but it was nonetheless a considerable improvement.
There were a few things in association with Calgary Centre to which we took exception. This was with regard to where the boundaries cut through existing communities. As a result of our feelings on this we made representation to the commission. I am pleased to say the commission accepted the recommendations we made. I suppose I feel that way because they did, but nonetheless I think it demostrates the responsiveness of the Alberta commission to reasonable suggestions. Therefore they should be applauded. Consequently in terms of the last issue of maps produced in January, in terms of my constituency and the city of Calgary in general, the map meets with the approval of the members and the people of the city, at least as far as I can see.
In the last minute before ten o'clock I wish to acknowledge the problem raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave), respecting the inability of our existing system to acknowledge the need for regional representation. This would acknowledge the fact that somehow there is a difference in terms of population within densely populated cities and within rural areas. Somehow that should be reflected in our system. That problem, and the fact that the committee of the House of Commons when looking at redistribution the last time overlooked this, constitute something that is unfortunate. One never knows the schedule of this House, but I hope that sometime in the not too distant future this House will address itself to the question of how we can provide representation in the House of Commons that is fair and equitable, taking into consideration regions, areas, remoteness from existing communications, travel centres, Ottawa, and so on.
I see that it is now ten o'clock. I merely want to repeat that in my opinion the commission for Alberta, given the existing act, has done a very credible job. I have to voice my approval of that.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST THAT DEPARTMENTAL CONTRACTS SPECIFY USE OF CANADIAN CERAMICS
TRANSPORT-REQUEST THAT DEPARTMENTAL CONTRACTS SPECIFY USE OF CANADIAN CERAMICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not often one gets to speak twice in a matter of half an hour,
The only way that small secondary industry is going to get ahead in Canada is if it receives the support in many cases of the federal government. An article in the March 6, 1976, edition of the Financial Post states that imports are strangling Canadian secondary industry. It is no wonder. A case in point was brought out by my question of December 12, 1975, when I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), and I quote:
Because of the comparative advantage we enjoy in the ceramics industry in Canada-
I am not so sure we can maintain this advantage if the government keeps acting in the manner it did with regard to the Calgary airport contract.
-will the minister, together with the Minister of Supply and Services and Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, assure this industry that government contracts will specify the use of available Canadian ceramic products and that we will not follow the practice followed in the case of the new Calgary airport?
The minister replied that the government observes some broad rules-and I emphasize the word broad-in connection with Canadian materials. He continued:
I do not know if they apply in the particular case in question, or to a specific tendering operation, but I will look into the matter.
The case I am referring to concerned the letting of tenders for ceramic tile for the new airport at Calgary. The specifications stated a Canadian tile should be used. Canadian tile and German tile were tested by the Alberta Research Council; both were deficient in some areas, but the German tile had more deficiencies. Then it was brought to the attention of the government that the specifications were more stringent than Canadian government specifications board standard No. 75-GP-1B. Subsequently, the tenders were issued on the revised specifications to which Canadian tile could subscribe. Tenders were submitted; Frontenac Tile and International Brick and Tile, both Canadian companies, and a Germany company submitted quotations, and International Brick and Tile was the lowest Canadian bid.
The architect stated he wanted German tile because he was familiar with it and would guarantee it. But the Research Council of Alberta had done extensive study and tests on Alberta tile, and had in fact helped set up the process and kilns and was prepared to stand behind it. The province of Alberta's minister of transport was prepared to give assurances as to the ability to deliver on time and would give written guarantees. Federal people on site
March 11, 1976

seemed satisfied at the time. However, after all these assurances the government gave the contract to a German company and based its decision on the uncertainty of deliverability. Unreal, Mr. Speaker!
I can only say that I hope that after the minister looks into this situation he will see that this does not happen again. International Brick and Tile now is making pottery and is intending to sell its tile kiln as it cannot get the reputation needed to break into local markets. The ceramic industry in Canada is viable and competitive, but it is just getting started and needs the kind of help that government can give it by awarding contracts for this type of tile to Canadian owned companies whenever possible, even if the process is a little more complicated.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member will be pleased to know that we have advised the Calgary project office to revise the specification to a Canadian government specifications board standard which had been developed in conjunction with Canadian industry. However, as it was too late to issue that change before tenders closed, the general contract was awarded but the contractor was instructed to obtain quotations on the revised specification and specifically to invite tenders from two Canadian manufacturers who had questioned the specification.
In the re-tendering, International Brick and Tile of Edmonton submitted an identical price to that of Darling-ton-Haskins and Company of Vancouver, the original low bidder who was supplying a tile manufactured in Germany. Both companies were asked to supply test reports to show that they could meet the CGBS standards. The Dar-lington-Haskins test exceeded the specification while International Brick and Tile were not able to furnish test reports. This company, Mr. Speaker, was in the process of developing a tile and had not yet produced one which would meet the standards. We have been in contact with them since, and as of October they still did not have satisfactory test results to show us. Therefore the contractor was authorized, on June 30, to place an order with Darlington-Haskins and Company for the supply of quarry tile in the interest of permitting the job to remain on schedule.
As a result of the above, its associated problems and other objectives of the ministry, the following actions are taking place. First, as a participant on the interdepartmental policy committee for the Government of Canada master specifications we are formulating a uniform course of action with all five member departments, Public Works, National Defence, Industry, Trade and Commerce, Indian Affairs and Northern Development and Transport with respect to both Treasury Board's policy and guidelines on contracting, and Ministry of Transport contract regulations on the use of Canadian products.
Second, the implementation of the use of the master specification for projects within the regions is at a high degree of achievement. An integral part of the master specifications is the standards which are set by the Canadian government specification board, which includes ceramic tile.

Finally, it is now mandatory for all consultants engaged by the Ministry of Transport to use the master specification exclusively.

speechtext:
When there was a fire at Greenwood, for example, the people at the base there, businessmen in the surrounding community, went into Halifax, sat down in the premier's office, called the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) and forced him to give a clear undertaking that nothing would happen to Greenwood. That is fine for Greenwood. But what do we do at Shearwater? Do we burn down the gymnasium? Do we burn down half of Dartmouth and then get on the phone to ask for some assurance that this base will not be so seriously disrupted in a precipitous way that the civilian employees and the surrounding economy will suffer unduly?
I have asked the government, if it insists on going ahead with widespread closures, to establish an interdepartmental committee within the cabinet which would take into account the sociology of the question, the background of the civilians concerned. I have pointed out that these men are, by the government's own definition, technology redundant people, people who would not in most cases have more than a 20 per cent opportunity of ever regaining permanent employment.
We need an interdepartmental committee, on top of which must be a cabinet committee, which would look at the sociological and economic impact of these moves, which would consider the relocation and retraining of those people with some humane concern. I find myself speaking here this evening because at the root of all this is clearly the avowed intention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to reduce the Canadian armed forces to a level below which they cannot posture as a defence force but merely as a para-military police force functioning in aid of the civil power. That is not good enough.

March 11, 1976
Adjournment Debate
So that my words of wisdom will fall clearly on all ears let me repeat them. When I first came to this Chamber ten or 11 years ago the armed forces had their share of the gross national product. They played their part in the ability of the country to grow. We maintained an adequate posture in the eyes of our neighbours to the south and our allies in Europe. We were able to play a meaningful part in collective continental defence and elsewhere. This had an influence on our export trade. We had good will, in other words. We were treated at a high level in respect of need to know. Ten years later we have lost access to partnership on a need to know basis.
Our Prime Minister is being told to put up or shut up. I find it offensive that anyone would have to speak that way to my Prime Minister. I would remind the members of this Chamber of that. These are matters of concern. I suggest that they are emphasized by the continuing rumours. We understand it is the clear intention of the Department of National Defence to submit to its minister, and subsequently to cabinet, a list of recommendations that will include not only the bases I have mentioned but possibly seven or eight more. These closures or consolidations will affect some 7,000 or 8,000 civilian employees, their wives and families, and the communities in which they live. We should not do this lightly. I wonder whether tonight we might hear more about when this report will be presented to the minister, when it will go to the cabinet, and what generally is the attitude of the government in respect of handling this very serious and important departmental report.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) said a few moments ago, it is not too often one has an opportunity to speak twice in this Chamber during a short period of time.
I was beginning to wonder whether the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) had a question or was merely making a speech. In any event I will try to meet some of the issues he raised. I must say I agree with him that most of the questions I have heard the hon. member put in the House are serious questions. I certainly understand his concern with regard to Shearwater and Greenwood. I would, however, like to try to correct a couple of misrepresentations of fact he made which I am
sure he did not make intentionally. Certainly the Premier of Nova Scotia did not have to force out of my minister a statement concerning the future status of Greenwood.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-POSSIBLE CLOSURE OF BASES IN NOVA SCOTIA-REQUEST FOR CONSULTATION WITH PROVINCIAL AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
I did read the Halifax Herald, but that is not necessarily the most credible voice in the country either. The situation of course is that the minister is endeavouring to use the budget of the department as wisely and efficiently as he possibly can. It is a well known fact that the armed forces have a very large overhead, so to speak, or infrastructure.
I must take issue with the hon. member's contention that it is the intention of our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to reduce our armed forces to a paramilitary force. That, of course, is patent nonsense. We have undoubtedly the most professional armed forces in the world today. We have one of the most efficient forces in the world. The fact is that the minister has asked within his department for a review of the infrastructure of the armed forces. He now has the report of the group that carried out the study. He is working on it at the present time. It has not been presented to cabinet and therefore no decisions have been made with regard to the closure of any base, the phase out or the reduction of any base to this date. There may well be some.
The hon. member's statement that seven or eight bases would be closed is probably a gross exaggeration. The statement that 7,000 or 8,000 employees would lose their jobs is also probably an exaggeration. The hon. member also suggested that an interdepartmental committee be established to look into the economic and social effects of this kind of government action on the communities involved. I want to tell the hon. member that such a committee exists. It was set up in the fall of 1974 or the spring of 1975, at my request to the Prime Minister after the closing of a military base in my constituency was announced.
In summary let me say that no decision has been made to close, reduce, or alter any base in the country. The minister has made no recommendations to cabinet to date, and therefore no decision can be made until cabinet considers the minister's recommendation.
